narrative:
The 2026 New York Mets entered the season with legitimate aspirations, buoyed by a blockbuster offseason that brought Juan Soto to Flushing. But the dream unraveled almost immediately. After a promising 3-2 start in March, April turned catastrophic — a 7-19 month that buried the team before the weather even warmed. Bullpen collapses, grand slams surrendered, and walk-off heartbreaks piled up at a pace that made even the most faithful Mets fans wince. By the end of April, New York was staring up at the rest of the division from a deep hole.

May offered a genuine lifeline. The Mets surged to a 16-12 record, their best month of the season, anchored by clutch contributions from Tyrone Taylor and a roster that suddenly started playing with something to prove. The offense found its rhythm, Soto began asserting himself, and for a brief stretch it looked like the kind of turnaround that Mets mythology is built on. June, however, was merciless — a 10-17 swoon driven in part by Kodai Senga's struggles and a bullpen that kept handing games away in the late innings.

July brought a split personality. A brutal month overall at 11-14, it nonetheless produced some of the season's most electric moments — none bigger than Soto's three-run blast on July 6th, the highest-leverage play of the entire season, which briefly reignited belief in a comeback. August stabilized things with a 15-12 record, the second winning month of the year, as Francisco Alvarez emerged as an offensive force and the team began playing with a loose, nothing-to-lose energy. September has been a 12-12 grind, the season finding its final equilibrium — a team talented enough to beat anyone on a given night, but not consistent enough to have climbed back into contention.

At 74-88, the 2026 Mets are a portrait of potential deferred. The pieces are here — Soto's power, Bichette's clutch hitting, Taylor's surprising pop, Alvarez's development — but the April hole proved too wide and too deep to escape. The rotation's inconsistency, particularly from Senga, and a bullpen that surrendered momentum at the worst moments defined a season that always felt one sustained run away from meaning something. As September winds down, the Mets are playing out the string, but the foundational talent gives reason to believe 2027 could be a different story entirely.

chapters.title: Opening Day Optimism Shattered
chapters.description: A promising March gives way to a historically bad April as the Mets' bullpen and rotation combine to bury them in the standings.

chapters.title: May Awakening
chapters.description: The Mets finally play winning baseball, with Tyrone Taylor's breakout home run and a reinvigorated offense providing the season's first sustained hope.

chapters.title: Summer Swoon
chapters.description: June and early July bring a familiar collapse, with the rotation faltering and the bullpen squandering leads in heartbreaking fashion.

chapters.title: Soto Takes Over
chapters.description: Juan Soto's monster three-run homer on July 6th becomes the defining moment of the season, sparking a stretch of clutch performances that briefly reignite the fanbase.

chapters.title: August Resilience
chapters.description: The Mets post their second winning month behind Francisco Alvarez's emergence and Tyrone Taylor's continued power surge, playing their most consistent baseball of the year.

chapters.title: September at .500
chapters.description: The Mets play out a .500 September — Bo Bichette delivers a stunning three-run homer and A.J. Ewing steps into the spotlight, hinting at what this roster might become.
